title: Shrink the coefficients
description: Course activity for Exercise 5: choose Linear Regression, Ridge, or Lasso and move the regularization strength (alpha) to see how a model's coefficients, predictions, and training/validation error change, on the same 360-feature cortical-thickness recipe used throughout the course.
instructions: Choose a model, then move alpha (regularization strength) on the log-scale slider or pick an exact value from the dropdown. Regularization adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients to the model's fitting objective; alpha controls how strong that penalty is. Watch the observed-vs-predicted plot, the coefficient bars, and the training/validation MSE update together. Linear Regression has no alpha -- it is shown as the unregularized baseline. Only training and validation numbers are shown here; the test set stays locked.
linearRegressionNote: Linear Regression has no regularization strength to set: it is the unregularized baseline shown for comparison. Choose Ridge or Lasso to use the alpha control.
coefficientDisplayNote: This chart shows a fixed set of the largest-magnitude standardized coefficients at the current alpha -- a display choice so the chart stays readable, not a second feature-selection step. All 360 features are used to fit every model shown here (except where Lasso has shrunk a coefficient to exactly zero).
reflectionPrompts: Switch between Ridge and Lasso at a similar validation MSE. Which one changes the number of nonzero coefficients, and which mostly keeps many small coefficients?
Increase alpha well past the best validation value for either model. What happens to the coefficient bars and to validation MSE?
A coefficient reaches exactly zero for Lasso at some alpha. Does that prove the corresponding brain region has nothing to do with age?
Should you choose alpha using the training curve or the validation curve? Why?
